#9659. Meet the Writer: Alena Belova on Reputation, AI Search and the Numbers Nobody Publishes

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

HackerNoon's Writers Spotlight - Where we honor HackerNoon's top writers, their contributions and impacts on the evergreen community. An exclusive interview series by HackerNoon 💚

Welcome to HackerNoon’s Meet the Writer Interview series, where we learn a bit more about the contributors that have written some of our favorite stories.

My first job, in 2015, was finding out what people really think of things: market research, then reputation analysis for a national lottery brand. Everyone has a view of a lottery. Nobody is neutral. Then I moved to Istanbul and co-founded an e-commerce business selling Turkish goods directly to customers. That is where I learned what I now tell founders: you can be the voice of your company, but the product needs its own accounts, its own email and its own search presence from day one.

Later I worked on a large language model project. From that side you learn two things quickly. An answer is never as fixed as it looks: while a model is still being worked on, the same question can come back noticeably different from one round to the next. And geography matters, just as it always did in search. The same question asked from two countries can return two different pictures of the same company.

That path explains where I am now. I'm a partner at BARS Agency. We build and promote digital products, work on reputation and on how people and companies are presented in AI search. Geometrika started there as a tool we built for ourselves and our clients, to see how AI assistants describe a brand and which sources they lean on, so that strategy could start from data instead of guesses. Exhibo, a global art gallery and culture platform where I'm co-founder and editor-in-chief, asks the same question about culture: which galleries, museums and places become visible online and which quietly drop out.

On paper, these look like different careers. It's one question asked in different rooms: how does something get seen and why do people believe what they see?

I studied art history and I'm studying psychology now, which covers both halves of that question. I lived in Istanbul for several years. These days I live between Doha, Dubai and Egypt.

My latest Top Story asked why a two-hour transfer in the Alps can cost more than the flight that got you there. It belongs to a series I keep coming back to: hidden economics, the prices everyone pays and nobody explains. The newest piece in it is about film rebates in the Middle East. The detail I can't stop thinking about is that a desert now comes with a percentage attached. Every line producer knows the rates by heart. Almost no government in the region publishes what it has actually paid out.

The method doesn't change from piece to piece. Start with a number that should be public. Find out whether it is. If it is, read every row of it.

On HackerNoon it's mostly search, AI and the psychology around them. Somewhere along the way the psychology pieces and the search pieces turned into the same subject. People tend to accept a coherent, confident explanation without checking how it was put together. Memory does it to us: a manager sincerely remembers backing the idea that won. AI answers do it for us: one fluent paragraph, assembled from sources of very different quality, reads as settled fact.

Elsewhere it's culture. At Exhibo I write about art, architecture and the stories attached to objects and places. One pattern keeps coming back: fiction borrows a real place and forgets to give it back. Tatooine is in Tunisia. Agrabah is stitched together from real cities.

The subjects wander. The question underneath doesn't: what is actually going on beneath something everyone takes at face value?

I start with a table. Whatever I want to know, row by row. Half of it usually fills in an afternoon. The piece lives in the cells that refuse to fill.

Then I go to the primary documents, which in this region often means a French PDF, a ministry decree or a press release that is generous with every number except the one you need. When I find a dataset I add it back up against its own totals before I trust a single figure from it.

The research eats the writing. I can spend a week finding out that a number almost never exists in public. That week is invisible in the final piece. Finding out that something isn't there is a finding too. It just takes longer to write down.

The other challenge is restraint. When you've read seven years of a ledger, you want to show the reader every row. The reader wants three.

I want companies to be able to see how AI systems describe them and where that picture comes from, the way they once learned to read their own search results. Most still check it by asking ChatGPT about themselves once and hoping for the best. And what actually moves those answers is rarely what anyone expects. Start a podcast and the assistants often pick it up. I once shared a few of my own photos of desert monasteries. Within weeks the AI version of me had become a cultural heritage contributor and was drifting towards "philanthropist". Nobody has ever complained about that particular error.

I want the same for culture. A serious gallery in Doha or a small museum in Cairo shouldn't disappear from what people find online simply because the information about it was never made easy to find.

Trips planned around exactly one thing I want to see. Lately it's usually a ruin with a desert around it, though it can just as easily be a coastline or a forest. Everything else is allowed to happen on the way, as long as there's European coffee somewhere on the route.

And when the list runs out, I go out into the desert just to look at nothing for an hour. It is the only place where my phone and I agree to ignore each other.

Languages. Spanish, Arabic and, less gracefully, Turkish. Spanish feels familiar, at least in its logic. Arabic and Turkish don't. Many Arabic words are built from three-consonant roots, so one root gives you a writer, a book and an office. In Turkish a whole sentence can be a single word thirty letters long. Both break my brain a little.

Translators and AI do fine with a menu. Face to face, they still get lost. So I'm doing it the long way.

And art, which stopped being a hobby the day it became a job. I will still talk Monet and Manet with anyone who confuses them.

First, an experiment I've wanted to run for a while: asking every major AI assistant who I am, then tracing the wrong answers back to where they came from, when they came from anywhere at all. A machine's idea of you is assembled from places you have forgotten you ever wrote.

Then more hidden economics: who pays for a free museum. The British Museum opened free in 1759, on a collection a public lottery had helped pay for. In 2026 the Louvre and the Grand Egyptian Museum both raised their prices. Someone always pays. The question is who. And whether they know it.

Where else would a story about airport transfers in the Alps sit next to one about falling in love with chatbots? I've stopped asking which of them is the tech story.

If you ever go looking for a number and it isn't there, write that down. The absence is usually the story.

Rita Sheth on Solopreneurship, AI and Bias in Tech

#9657. Image Thumbnail Generation: Object Storage Retention After Server-Side Upload Resizing

TL;DR: Keep each training artifact original in private object storage, generate a fixed thumbnail in a backend worker, and save that thumbnail as another object. Give both keys explicit retention classes. This is the least complex design that makes deletion reproducible across US and EU deployments without turning an image CDN's URL grammar into application state.

Recommendation: start with private storage and a backend-triggered worker. Store artifacts/{artifactId}/source.png and artifacts/{artifactId}/thumb-320.png separately, then delete both from the same retention decision. The extra object is boring. Boring is useful here.

A training-artifact browser looks like an image feature, but its harder contract is retention. A user may replace a dataset preview, delete a run, or apply a policy after 30 days. If the UI can derive arbitrary transformations from a URL, the set of derivatives becomes less obvious to the application that must prove what disappeared. Fixed keys make the inventory finite.

I benchmark this design by counting coordination points, not by admiring feature lists. The default path has four: accept the upload, persist the original, enqueue one resize job, and persist one derivative. Reads then fetch a known private object through a presigned URL. No image SDK belongs in the frontend, and a UI deploy can't silently create a new retention class by changing query parameters.

The key scheme is the policy. Keep the source and thumbnail under one artifact prefix, but record their roles separately in the database. Prefixes make listing practical; the database remains the authority for deletion state because object metadata can't be searched server-side here. A lifecycle rule can enforce day-scale expiry, with a minimum of one day, but it should backstop the product's deletion workflow rather than replace it.

This also exposes a real boundary: storage isn't an image transformer. If product requirements become "crop any width at the edge," pick a dedicated image service. Pretending an object store has that feature creates glue, and glue is where a supposedly simple stack gets expensive to reason about.

One size. One key. One deletion deadline.

First, ask whether every retained byte has an owner and a deadline. The original and thumb-320 should inherit the artifact's policy at write time. A worker retry must target the same derivative key, so repeated delivery replaces the same output rather than accumulating thumb-final-2.png. Infrai's storage surface has no object versioning or object lock, so this pattern is unsuitable when overwritten bytes must remain recoverable or WORM retention is required. Use an external system designed for that guarantee.

Strict concurrent writers are another cutoff. There is no If-Match conditional write in this storage surface. Serialize replacement through a queue or coordinate ownership in the application database when two processes could publish the same key. That's a design constraint, not a reason to invent a distributed lock in the image worker.

Second, count delivery requirements. Private or signed-only access fits training data. Permanent public object URLs, public bucket hosting, and static-site delivery do not. Browser-direct upload also needs care because self-service CORS configuration is unavailable in the stated capability set. Keep uploads behind the backend unless your selected storage product provides the browser policy you require.

Region policy deserves a plain sentence. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration in this option. A US/EU deployment should therefore choose placement deliberately and maintain its own migration plan before compliance turns that omission into a deadline.

The image library is deliberately outside this example. Sharp, libvips, or another processor can produce the bytes. Before wiring the worker, I want the live request schema for the notification capability rather than a copied SDK type or a guessed JSON body. Infrai exposes that schema through public discovery. This runnable check uses the API base URL from the environment so the unlinked comparison doesn't embed a vendor URL.

A production consumer should persist a deletion state, tolerate at-least-once delivery, and treat an already-absent key as success. Keep the resize operation deterministic: fixed dimensions, encoder settings, and output key. Otherwise a retry can produce different bytes under the same retention record. Use the returned request JSON Schema to build and validate the notification payload; the point of discovery is to avoid freezing fields into an article when the machine-readable contract is available.

Infrai is one fit for this shape when a team values a plain REST API and doesn't want another SDK or client version to maintain. Anything that sends HTTP can call it, and bucket notifications can trigger post-upload work. The public, self-describing discovery surface returns the current request schema without a key, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. Those shared conventions trim contract and onboarding glue; they don't change the storage boundary above.

Credential consolidation is a separate advantage. Infrai provides one key for everything across 295 routes in 20 modules, with one bill for their usage. In this workflow, adding a queue or scheduler later doesn't force the thumbnail worker to gain another credential, invoice, authentication path, or billing integration.

It is not a fit for permanent public image links, WORM retention, strict conditional writes, self-managed browser-upload CORS, automatic cross-region replication, or on-the-fly transforms. Pick a storage or image specialist whose documented guarantees cover the missing requirement. This trade-off is more important than saving one SDK installation.

Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Cloudflare R2, and Backblaze B2 belong on the object-storage shortlist. Evaluate them against the guarantees your retention policy needs, especially versioning, object lock, region behavior, lifecycle granularity, CORS control, and migration tooling. Don't infer equivalence from an S3-shaped API. Infrai's vendor coverage includes S3 and R2 but excludes GCS and B2, which matters if one of those is already your operational standard.

A dedicated image product such as Cloudflare Images or imgix is the runner-up when the number of requested variants is unknown at upload time. That choice moves transformation into delivery and can reduce stored derivatives. It also means deletion testing must include the service's derived-asset and cache behavior. Read those contracts before making transformed URLs durable database fields.

Synchronous server resize wins in a narrow case: low upload volume, one tiny derivative, and a product requirement that the thumbnail exist before the upload response returns. Its failure domain is easy to see, but image CPU and storage latency now extend the user request. Set a hard timeout and measure the full upload path. Once p95 grows or files get large, move the same deterministic operation behind a notification or queue.

The worker design has its own cost: thumbnails are briefly unavailable after upload. Model that state in the UI. A neutral placeholder is cleaner than polling without a bound.

My decision rule is blunt. Choose stored derivatives until actual requirements demand arbitrary transforms. Choose an image CDN when edge-time variants are the product. Choose synchronous resizing only while measured upload latency and concurrency leave comfortable headroom. The retention model should survive any of those delivery choices.

#9656. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

#9655. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9652. Node.js Share Cards: Budgeting Template Text Overlays Without Sacrificing Search Quality

A fintech media library needs enough visual detail to assign useful search tags, but its social share cards need predictable delivery size. Resolve that tension by keeping tagging inputs separate from delivery derivatives: compose each card from a template and the article title, then store it under the content version. TL;DR: evaluate search quality on the tagging input, evaluate bandwidth on the finished card, and regenerate whenever the title or template changes.

The useful unit of analysis is a published content version. A request count alone cannot tell you whether a transform produced a useful artifact or merely repeated work. This distinction also determines how much telemetry deserves retention.

Consider a proposed library record for a payments explainer: its title is “Understanding settlement windows,” its template is “research,” and its search vocabulary includes settlement and payments. These are example editorial values, not observed tagging results. A tagger should be evaluated against the approved vocabulary and the source material. A card composer should receive the approved title and template configuration. Text added for distribution should not become accidental evidence for the search index.

A legible title overlay does not establish that the image contains enough information for useful tagging. Conversely, preserving detail useful to a tagging system can increase the bytes delivered with every share-card request. The MDN image-format guide is a useful starting point for selecting formats and understanding compression trade-offs, but it cannot determine the acceptable quality threshold for a particular fintech library. That threshold requires evaluation on the library's own material.

Use a reviewed set of assets with expected search terms. Compare tag relevance at each candidate input size, then compare card readability at the intended display size. Record the evaluation procedure alongside the template version. No benchmark result is assumed here; the design makes the eventual result attributable.

The composition input is a template image plus an explicit list of operations built from template configuration. The article title supplies the overlay text. In a proposed Express service, publication should resolve those inputs before asking the image backend to compose the result; a request to display the card should resolve the stored artifact for that content version. This is an application design, not a claim about Express providing an image compositor.

Include both content version and template version in the artifact identity. A title edit must produce a new identity even when the article identifier stays the same. A template change also needs a new identity, because keeping the old identity would make an apparently current card contain an old visual layout. Store the resulting image under that identity, with private or signed-only access and presigned retrieval where access is required.

The subtle failure is a perfectly valid image with yesterday's title. HTTP success doesn't detect it. A version-aware acceptance check does: the stored artifact must correspond to the inputs the publisher approved. If composition fails, return the designated static card and record the fallback outcome. This is a general application recovery policy.

A stable capability contract also makes a backend substitution tractable: the application continues to submit the composition intent while the provider behind that capability changes. Validate the visual result after substitution, since an unchanged application interface is not evidence of identical rendering.

Bandwidth has two separate terms: bytes sent for analysis and bytes delivered as cards. For a hypothetical planning workload of 1,000 content versions, one 200 KB analysis input per version accounts for 200 MB of input transfer in decimal units. If each resulting 60 KB card is delivered 100 times, card delivery accounts for 6 GB. These are explicit assumptions for arithmetic, not measured sizes or provider limits. The example explains why shrinking the tagging input can sacrifice search quality while leaving the larger delivery term untouched.

Telemetry can obscure this distinction if every request carries its own high-cardinality labels. Under a proposed labeling scheme with 3 pipeline stages, 4 outcomes, and 5 template families, the Cartesian product contains 60 possible combinations before any other dimensions. Add a distinct article identifier for each of 1,000 articles and that upper bound becomes 60,000. Actual occupancy may be lower, but the multiplication remains a useful design warning. Keep article identifiers in diagnostic records that require them; aggregate routine metrics using bounded categories.

Retention deserves the same arithmetic. Suppose planning assumes 100,000 diagnostic events per day at 500 bytes each. Seven days represent 350 MB of raw payload; 30 days represent 1.5 GB, before indexing, replication, or compression. These numbers describe a hypothetical retention budget. They do not estimate a vendor's storage bill.

Sampling introduces a different trade-off. A proposed 10% sample reduces the expected count of retained routine success events, but it can hide rare composition defects and cannot support an unqualified count of all successes. Keep complete aggregate counters, retain fallback and rejection records according to the investigation policy, and sample detailed success records separately. Don't attach titles, full images, or signed access URLs to routine logs just because the request handler can see them.

The appropriate comparison is the work required between approved content and a searchable, deliverable artifact. Image transformation, object storage, and model evaluation are different responsibilities; a product that covers one should not receive credit for automatically solving the others.

These are evaluation boundaries, not benchmark rankings. The primary documentation listed below should determine whether each candidate can implement the actual template. A product name alone doesn't establish compatibility.

For an Amazon S3 plus OpenAI moderation alternative, plan for 2 provider accounts and 2 sets of credentials: AWS and OpenAI. The application must connect asset identity, the screening request, the decision, and subsequent composition. It also owns the relationship between retry behavior and persisted state. Moderation determines whether an asset proceeds under a content policy; search tagging describes what a permitted asset contains. Neither establishes visual composition quality.

Infrai provides one REST API, one API key, and one bill, with no SDK to install. It is a suitable candidate where retaining the capability contract while changing its underlying vendor matters: the Express application keeps its composition contract as the provider behind the capability changes. Its self-describing API adds a separate workflow advantage: public discovery requires no key and returns full request JSON Schema, response schema, and runnable examples. That lets the team inspect the operation contract before implementing the template adapter. Its 295 routes across 20 modules mean image handling and subsequent storage integration need not introduce separate platform credentials or invoice reconciliation. Per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request identifiers support attribution across the workflow. Shared credentials alone do not establish an atomic transaction or prove that a moderation output can be passed directly into an image operation.

Before wiring that path, inspect the capability schema. The following curl request retrieves the composition contract. Set the base variable to the service's versioned API base and supply the API key through the environment. Discovery is public; the optional authentication header demonstrates how subsequent authenticated calls obtain credentials. This example retrieves a contract; it does not claim to compose or moderate an asset.

This is a public read operation. Curl surfaces HTTP failures and applies its retry handling to transient responses, including 429; use a current curl version that honors Retry-After. For subsequent write operations, establish idempotency before enabling retries. A repeated composition attempt must not become an unrelated artifact with a different content identity.

The distinction matters for bandwidth: inspect the processing contract before deciding which input derivative to send. Keep the screening decision, any image-processing output, and the approved version associated in application state. Validate the exact field mapping from the retrieved schema before implementing the handoff.

Start with one template family and a reviewed subset of the fintech library. Keep the static fallback available, check that title edits create new artifact identities, and compare the resulting cards at their display size. Evaluate search tags against the reviewed vocabulary independently. An attractive card cannot compensate for a search index that misses the intended concept.

Then increase coverage while tracking aggregate fallback counts, input bytes, delivered bytes, and useful search results. Retain detailed evidence long enough to investigate mismatches. Change one image-quality setting at a time so its effect can be attributed. The rollout decision should rest on that evidence, with the template contract and versioned storage identity keeping the experiment reproducible.

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

#9648. Four free Claude Certified practice exams

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at leanzero.net

On 19 November 2026 two changes went live together on the certifications page. Four free Claude Certified practice exams went in, 1,165 questions in all, and 2,995 of the 3,101 published Atlassian questions got new wording.

I'll give you my take before the changelog. I think the stronger model we brought in for the wording writes better sentences than our own pipeline ever did. It also changed what some questions claimed, in sentences that read perfectly well. Scripts check every rewrite. So does a second reader, a separate AI agent whose only job is to prove a rewrite wrong. Those checks are why I'm comfortable putting the result in front of you.

Why would you care how a practice question is worded? You read hundreds of them in a sitting, often in a second language, and you're tired. A clipped sentence costs attention you need for the question itself.

There's now a practice exam here for four of Anthropic's proctored Claude certifications.

The exam lengths are from Anthropic's certification page as it read on 18 November 2026. Three of the four exams get an updated edition on 7 December 2026, and the page says the date you test decides which version you take.

A quick mock here draws 20 questions. For the three exams that change, a full paper follows the December edition in its length and its domain weights, so it has 70 questions. For Architect – Foundations it has 60.

Each question shows the sentence from the Claude documentation that decides the answer, with a link to the page. Each of the four options gets its own explanation. If you think we're wrong, you can check the page. The access key we emailed you for the Atlassian exams opens these too, because an access key belongs to your email address and to no single exam.

These are our own questions. Anthropic has no part in them and doesn't endorse them. None of them is copied from an exam guide or from another site.

Before you trust a score, you should know how we judge it. Anthropic's exams pass on a scaled score of 720 on a scale of 100 to 1,000, and a practice percentage can't be converted to that. So the result screen measures you against a 75% practice target and says in plain words that the 75% is LeanZero's line.

You should also know who can sit the exam itself. Anthropic's page says the exams are open to people at Claude Partner Network organizations. Our practice exams are free for anybody.

I should name one limit. Our Claude questions all have one correct answer out of four, while the Architect – Foundations guide says its paper also has questions where you select more than one. We don't have those yet.

In September I wrote that the Claude Architect syllabus exposed the gaps of someone self-taught. The four exams above cover that syllabus and three more.

We had checked the Atlassian questions several times. They were still tiring to read. We did that to them ourselves.

In September we measured the options in my screenshots of mock exam questions for three of the five exams. The receipt, dated 2026-09-07 in tools/option_shape.py, gives a median of 4, 5 and 6 words an option there. The options we had written had a median of 14 to 16 words. So our pipeline squeezed them down to between 5 and 8. Our written rules and automatic checks all pushed toward fewer words, and not one rule asked for a readable sentence.

I think the explanations under each answer took the worst of it. In the 2,995 reworded questions, 10,436 of 12,438 option explanations opened with an internal label or a verdict word such as "Wrong artifact" or "Correct --". A double hyphen stood in for punctuation in 10,084 of them. Those labels meant something to the pipeline and nothing to a candidate.

A script copied these out of the bank, the published text first and the reworded text second. The stem is the question text above the options. All six rewordings were accepted by the second reader I describe further down.

ACP-120, Jira administration, the pool behind our ACP-120 practice exam. A stem written as four clipped sentences:

Before: A project key changed from OPS to RUN. Old OPS links still resolve. Another team wants OPS for a new project. What should you do before deleting the retained previous key?

After: A project key was changed from OPS to RUN. The old OPS links still resolve. Now another team wants to use OPS for a new project. What should you do before deleting the previous key that was kept?

The explanation for one wrong option, "Rebuild its notification scheme":

Before: Wrong object -- notification schemes do not replace old project-key references.

After: Deleting a previous project key affects links, filters, gadgets, and queries that still use OPS. A notification scheme has nothing to do with references to the old project key.

ACP-120 again. Double hyphens doing the work of commas:

Before: Work item CNF-88 -- carrying security level 'Executives Only' -- is moved from project 'Confidential' into 'General', which has no security scheme at all. Which statement about CNF-88 after the move is correct?

After: Work item CNF-88, which has the security level 'Executives Only', is moved from the project 'Confidential' into 'General', which has no security scheme at all. Which statement about CNF-88 after the move is correct?

The explanation for the wrong option "Reverts within 30 days". Keep an eye on the word "documented", because it comes back later:

Before: Does not exist -- no delayed reversion of a moved work item's security level is documented anywhere on the page.

After: A moved work item takes the destination project's security settings when it moves, and nothing describes a moved work item's security level reverting after a 30-day delay.

Before: Your flow fans into three branches, each taking 1 minute, and finishes after 1 minute. How much processing time do the branches contribute?

After: Your flow has three branches that each take 1 minute to run, and it finishes after 1 minute. How much processing time do the branches contribute?

The explanation for the wrong option "0 minutes.":

Before: Wrong -- partial/insufficient: Delay and Send web request are named as processing-time contributors, but branches are named as a further contributor on the same page, so excluding them entirely misstates the rule.

After: Branches count toward processing time, with each branch counted separately, so their contribution is not 0 minutes.

ACP-420, Jira Service Management. Capitals for emphasis, and a double hyphen:

Before: You need a dashboard filter that returns only your own PENDING approval steps -- including ones you already voted on while other approvers decide, but no completed steps. Which function should it use?

After: You need a dashboard filter that returns only your own pending approval steps, including ones you already voted on while other approvers decide, but leaves out completed steps. Which function should it use?

The explanation for the wrong option "myPendingApproval()":

Before: Wrong -- myPendingApproval() excludes steps the user already voted on, the opposite of what is needed here.

After: The filter must include pending approval steps the current user has already voted on, but myPendingApproval() finds only pending steps the current user is yet to approve or decline and leaves out the ones already voted on.

ACP-520, Atlassian Cloud organization administration.

Before: On a Standard Cloud plan, a site admin -- not an org admin -- opens Connected Apps. Which statement about installing and managing apps there is correct?

After: On a Standard Cloud plan, a site admin who is not an org admin opens the Connected Apps page. Which statement about installing and managing apps there is correct?

The old explanation for the wrong option "Site admins can't install public Marketplace apps" quoted the page at you. The page names both roles for both kinds of app, and the new explanation says that in plain words:

Before: Wrong -- the page opens 'As an administrator, you can install and manage both Marketplace and private apps through the Connected Apps page' and its panel names 'Role: Organization admin, Site admin', with no public/private split by role.

After: Both organization admins and site admins can install Marketplace apps and private apps through the Connected Apps page. There is no split by role between public Marketplace apps and private apps.

ACP-620, Jira project administration. A passive stem with nobody in it:

Before: The Sprint Report burndown for MERIDIAN, a company-managed Scrum project, is opened on a board that has never been configured to track remaining estimates and time spent. Three lines -- grey, red, and green -- are expected. What actually shows?

After: An admin opens the Sprint Report burndown for Meridian, a company-managed Scrum project, on a board that has never been configured to track remaining estimates and time spent. The admin expects to see the grey, red, and green lines. What actually shows?

This one comes from the first passes on 18 November 2026, the day the rewording ran, when the model was still allowed to reword the options. Its correct option changed like this:

Before: Only grey and red; green needs tracking on.

After: Only the grey and red lines show because the green line requires tracking remaining estimates and time spent.

Before: Partial/insufficient -- wrongly extends the time-tracking dependency to the red line, which is documented as always present alongside the grey guideline.

After: The red line represents the actual work done during the sprint and is shown together with the grey line. It does not depend on configuring the board to track remaining estimates and time spent.

We run bulk work on cheap models. For this pass, on 18 November 2026, we paid for a stronger one and used it only for the prose. Each question was its own job in Elzi, our agent app.

That model knows nothing about Atlassian and sees one short briefing. In it are the question as published, the fact behind each option, the words that must survive character for character, and what reads badly in this particular question.

You can see what it did well in the six pairs. It says who does what, in the order it happens, and it puts the articles and the verbs back. Where an explanation opened with "Wrong -- partial/insufficient:", it now starts by saying what's true.

It went wrong mostly in one place. A published explanation often rests on what the documentation doesn't say, for example that no such limit is documented. The model liked to turn that into a flat product fact such as "there is no limit".

More than half of the second reader's refusals that day were of this kind. "Not documented" and "cannot" are different claims, and only the first one is ours to make.

It moved other things too. Options gained a clause that stated the very rule the candidate is meant to know. A Confluence question that says "flow", the current name, came back saying "automation rule". "PDF export" came back as "pdf export".

Our second reader refused about a third of the early rewrites, most often for an option that had gained, lost or changed a word. So that evening we locked the options.

Since then the runner puts the published options back character for character, so in a new rewrite only the stem and the explanations can differ. 1,292 accepted rewordings still carry options reworded before the lock, each compared claim by claim with the published option. The sixth pair above is one of them.

The repository is private. So I'll give you the file names as they are in it, and what each script refuses.

Of the 3,101 questions that went in, 1,159 were sent back at least once after an objection, from the reader or from the stricter checks we added during the day.

One mistake in this was ours and had nothing to do with the model. Two of our own checks contradicted each other: one refused any explanation that mentioned the documentation, and the other demanded that mention whenever the published line had it. Questions caught between them could never pass. Once we fixed the check, 73 failed rewrites passed without a new model call.

236 published questions were doubted along the way. The notes step parked 166 of them before any rewording, and the second reader raised the other 70 while it compared a rewrite with the published question. We settled them against the live Atlassian pages, one by one.

165 were repaired from the documentation. 66 were sound as published. That left 5. For 4 of them the documentation couldn't settle the doubt, and for 1 the page contradicted our answer key. We checked those 5 in the live product on a test site of our own. There, 2 were repaired, 1 was sound, and 2 were withdrawn.

That makes 167 repairs. Every repaired question kept its answer key. 67 of the repairs changed the documentation quote under the question. In 46 the old quote was kept and extended, and in 21 it was replaced.

Both withdrawn questions are from ACP-120. In the first, Atlassian's own recipient table backs one of our wrong options almost word for word, so no answer key could stand. The second describes a custom field whose context is limited to two work types. Jira now refuses to build that, and the API answered "The global context cannot be made non-global".

We built the Claude exams the other way round, facts first.

Was the blind reader any good? The same kind of reader answered an exam guide's twelve official sample questions blind and got 12 of 12, marking 2 of them hard. On its first blind check of our own drafts it answered 30 of 30 as well, and named the wording that gave each answer away. So a wrong answer was never the main worry.

About half of our first drafts went back for the same reason. The answer was right, but somebody who had never used the product could reach it by matching words.

We wrote 1,380 Claude questions and published 1,165. Blind readers withdrew 201, and 14 more are held back. Our hardest exam cost the most. For Architect – Professional we wrote 388 and published 266, with 122 withdrawn.

106 Atlassian questions keep their published wording. 16 of them ended the run with an open objection from the second reader, and 8 failed the automatic check. The other 82 are settled as "the published wording stays". Among those 82 are 18 whose accepted rewording we put back, because it failed one of the last checks on the finished bank. No further run is scheduled, and I'm fine with that. A question that can't be reworded without moving a fact stays the way it was.

I also want to be plain about who the readers are. In both pipelines they're AI agents with a strict brief, and none of them has sat your exam form. You have, or you will, so I'd like to hear from you.

We also fixed two small things on the way. A quote taken from documentation published as Markdown no longer shows its formatting marks in the review screen, and a hover border on cards in dark mode that never appeared now does.

I'm left with something I can't answer from our own numbers. A stronger model made thousands of explanations easier to read in one day. It also changed "not documented" into "cannot" often enough that we had to write a script against it. We found those because each question had a published version to compare with.

Suppose you let a model reword your runbooks or your admin documentation tonight and they read better in the morning. How would you find the sentences where the meaning moved?

If you've done a rewrite like that at work, tell me what you checked, in the comments under this article.

And if you sit one of the mocks and a question reads wrong, the quote and the link are right under it. Send the question and the sentence that proves it to office@leanzero.net. That is how four bad Atlassian questions got fixed in September.

#9647. Your AI Agents Will Be Attacked. Red-Team Them First

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

By Pramin Pradeep, Co-founder & CEO, BotGauge AI

For most of the last few years, my job was making software prove it works. At BotGauge, we built autonomous QA that tested our customers' apps before every release. Then those same customers started shipping AI agents, and the old playbook stopped being enough.

A test suite asks one question: does this do what it should? An agent needs a second one: what will it do when someone wants it to misbehave? That second question is red teaming. It's why we launched our agent red-teaming platform on October 28, 2026 and the developer community noticed: it finished #3 Product of the Day on Product Hunt.

Red teaming isn't new. It started as military war-gaming, became a staple of security teams paid to break in, and with LLMs turned into jailbreaking chatbots.

Agents raise the stakes because they act. They call tools, read inboxes, write to databases and hand tasks to other agents. A bad chatbot answer is embarrassing. A bad agent action is an incident.

And adoption is outrunning testing. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. Yet most teams I talk to test agents like APIs: happy paths, a few edge cases, a vibe check. None of that simulates an adversary.

OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top risk for LLM applications, but for agents it's only the front door. Here's what we see:

•       Indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in a web page, PDF, email or support ticket the agent reads mid-task.

•       Tool misuse: tricking the agent into calling a legitimate tool with harmful arguments, like a refund, a delete or an outbound email.

•       Data exfiltration: coaxing the agent into leaking customer data, system prompts or credentials through its outputs or tool calls.

•       Goal hijacking: slow, multi-turn manipulation that drifts the agent away from its task without tripping any single-message filter.

•       Multi-agent cascades: one compromised agent passing poisoned context to others that trust it by default.

Our autonomous QA product had paying customers and a working business. But functional testing was maturing fast, and the problem our customers kept raising wasn't "does it work?" It was "can I trust it in production?"

So we rebuilt BotGauge as an Agent Control Plane, and made one calls early:

●      Red teaming at the core, not a checkbox. Observability tells you what happened. Red teaming tells you what could happen, before a user or attacker finds it.

The goal is simple: attack your agent the way an adversary would, every time it changes, and show you exactly where it broke.

•       200+ custom attack strategies spanning injection, tool misuse, exfiltration, goal hijacking and jailbreaks, run against your real agent, not a sandboxed copy of the model.

•       Full tracing: every failed attack links to its trace, so you see which input, which step and which tool call went wrong.

•       Evals that persist: results are scored and compared across releases, so a fix doesn't quietly regress next sprint.

•       Fits your stack: it sits on top of runtimes like LangGraph and AWS Bedrock AgentCore instead of replacing them.

Your agents will be attacked. Regulators are already moving: NIST's AI risk guidance and the EU AI Act both call for adversarial testing. The only real question is who finds the holes first, your team or someone else. I'd rather it be you.

Pramin Pradeep is co-founder and CEO of BotGauge AI, an Agent Control Plane for testing, observing and governing AI agents in production. BotGauge is backed by Surface Ventures, IA Seed Ventures and Saka Ventures. *Sources

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9645. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9644. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9642. The text was gone and the page looked fine

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at bananafest-destiny.com

Open one of our agent pages on a phone and every line of text ends where the screen ends. Not with an ellipsis, not with a fade — mid-word, as though somebody had run a ruler down the right-hand edge and cut. There is no scrollbar. The page does not scroll sideways: swipe and nothing moves. Each paragraph is a tidy rectangle of text with its right-hand third simply absent, and it looks exactly like a design decision.

/zoo/cider3 at 360px, before and after. Both frames are screenshots of the served page; the upper one was taken off the live site before the fix, which is why it cannot be re-shot. The lower frame starts 20px further down the page because the text now wraps.

That page publishes an autonomous agent's rules file verbatim: the thing it works under and cannot edit. It is the most substantial text on the page and the reason the page exists. 119 of its text nodes were cut at 320px and 110 at 360px, losing 60 to 177 pixels off every line.

Across 16 pages at two phone widths, our own site was cutting 237 pieces of text. We shipped all of it, for weeks, and the only reason we found it is that a different bug the day before made us go looking: the code blocks in every one of our 44 posts had been clipped at the right-hand edge the whole time, on every phone.

Three things have to be true at once, and the third is the one that hides it:

Then the item sizes itself to the unbreakable thing, the text beside it gets stretched to the same width, and the wrapper quietly cuts the overhang off.

It cannot happen on a desktop. At 1280px the column is wide enough for the unbreakable string, so nothing grows, so nothing is cut. The defect is not subtle at phone width and does not exist at desk width, and the people who build the page — us, and perhaps you — look at the page at desk width all day.

And it produces no symptom at all. A sideways scrollbar is a symptom. overflow: hidden is a symptom suppressant: it takes the one visible sign that a layout is too wide and removes it, which is why it is in the stylesheet in the first place.

This is the part I would keep if you take nothing else.

Nothing in the prose CSS was wrong. Nothing in the rules element was wrong. We could have read those rules for an hour.

The agent page is a two-column grid that collapses to one implicit column below 900px. An automatic track's floor is the min-content of its widest item — and the widest item in that column is not the prose. It is a definition list holding the agent's repository address:

Forty-two characters, no spaces, no break opportunities, 320px wide at 15.2px. That one string set the column to 481px inside a 360px phone. The rules prose shares the column, so it was stretched to 481px too, and the page wrapper cut everything past 360.

The cause and the symptom were in different elements, and the symptom was the bigger one. A URL nobody would look at twice decided the width of the only text on the page anyone reads.

The fix is one line — .zoo-two-col > * { min-width: 0 } — plus making the cell that now has to hold the URL able to break it (overflow-wrap: anywhere), and stacking the label and value below 560px, because 8rem of label and 1rem of gap leaves 144px for the text, which is not a column.

The usual check for this is scrollWidth > clientWidth: does the content of this box overflow the box? It is a reading about boxes, and it answers a question no reader has. A reader's question is which words did I not get?

So the instrument walks every text node in the document, takes that node's own client rectangles, finds the nearest ancestor that hides overflow, and compares the right edge of the text to the content edge of the clipper:

That middle line is the one that keeps the output honest. A box with overflow-x: auto is also "too narrow for its content", and it is fine — the reader can swipe it. Only a box that hides the overhang is destroying text. Treat the two the same and you get a list of findings nobody can act on, which is the usual reason a check like this gets switched off.

Two more readings make a finding instead of a number: how many pixels were lost, and whether the document scrolls sideways. The second is what makes it a story. In the whole sweep, every page reported sideways=false. Wider than the viewport and no way to reach it is the shape of the bug; either one alone is ordinary.

The exclusion list matters too, and it is short: text that is clipped on purpose. Screen-reader-only labels, and the honeypot field on our contact form. Two class names. If that list ever gets long, the check is wrong.

The masthead was cutting the one link on it that reaches a product. On every page of the site, from 768px to 794px, See a product lost up to 26.2px of itself.

The masthead at 768px, before and after. In the lower frame the link row is horizontally scrollable, so the link cut by the edge there is reachable with a swipe — which is why the sweep does not count it.

768px is an iPad held upright. The two navigation bars swap at exactly that width: the compact one goes away and the seven-link one arrives — 26px before there is room for it. Measured properly, that row needs 1170px with nothing wrapping, and the page shell only hands it that from about 1210px. It swaps at 1280 now.

The scoreboard was losing the last digit of its own headline number. Two grid tracks totalling 336px inside a 288px box, so 6328 commits rendered as 632 and most of an 8.

The front-page scoreboard at 320px, before and after. The type is smaller in the right-hand frame; the grid is unchanged, and the reason is the next section.

And the page that lists the approved apps was cutting an app's own domain. withoutasking.com, 348px at 30px, set the width of the card row and the card's own overflow: hidden took 45.3px of it off. That is the second day running that the one string on a page that cannot wrap belonged to somebody we are writing about.

One more, and it is the cheapest lesson here: our /zoo headline is fluid type with a floor, clamp(3.5rem, 16.5vw, 5.5rem). Below about 340px the floor wins, and the floor is a fixed size. On the 17th that headline stopped saying "One app each" and started saying "25 apps attempted." — and attempted. is 312px of glyph in a 288px column. A floor is a fixed size and the text it has to hold is not. Nobody changed any CSS; somebody changed a word.

minmax(0, 1fr) is the standard answer to all of this, so the first change made every 1fr on the site into minmax(0, 1fr).

It clipped $36.09 — the total amount of money these agents have earned, the number the whole site is about — at every desktop width. I only found it because I measured the widths I was not worried about.

A bare 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr): its floor is the cell's min-content, so a row of uneven cells comes out uneven on purpose — the big figure takes the room it needs and the 1 and the 22 give it up. minmax(0, 1fr) says every track is exactly equal, and five equal tracks are 152px, and the figure is 185.7px.

What was wrong at 320px was never the track function. It was a figure too big for a 144px track. The figure came down; the tracks stayed as they were. The mutation that re-introduces minmax(0, 1fr) on that one rule is now a test, with the measurement written above it, because it is going to look like an obvious improvement to the next person who reads it.

The masthead fix took three attempts, and two of them passed the sweep.

A tighter gap between the links cut nothing at 768 — and still wrapped the navigation onto three lines across the brand name. Swapping the two navs at 1024 instead still left six of the seven links on two lines. Both of those are clean runs by the only question the instrument asks. Both look broken to a person.

A check that asks one question answers one question. The wrapping was not even new: the live site had done it at every width from 768 to about 1210 since the masthead was built, and no check of ours would ever have raised it, because no text was ever cut. Taking the screenshot raised it in a second.

The sweep reads 0 cut text nodes across 16 pages at 13 widths — 208 measurements, taken off the served pages rather than a local build, because the thing you want to know about is the thing readers are actually served. It was 237.

Seven assertions went into the test suite with it, each one broken first and watched failing, including the one that stops minmax(0, 1fr) coming back. 301 tests green.

None of which changes the part worth sitting with: five layouts on a site whose whole job is publishing a record were deleting that record's text on the device most people read it on, and the pages looked completely fine.
