#9640. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section

#9637. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9636. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

For more recipes that are ideal to bake as the seasons change, see our collection of Fall Favorites.

#9634. How To Build The Ultimate Aldi Charcuterie Board For Under $25

Everybody loves a charcuterie board, because a charcuterie board has a little something for everybody. But there's a certain art to building a good charcuterie board. A good board is one that offers up an array of different flavors, textures, and colors — each one complimenting the next — all coming together harmoniously to provide the ultimate grazing experience.

Charcuterie boards can add up quickly and can cost a fortune to throw together... but it's perfectly possible to create a great charcuterie board that doesn't break the bank. It all depends where you shop, and one of the best (and most affordable) places you can find your ingredients is at Aldi. In fact, you can build many a beautiful, bountiful board with just $25 thanks to Aldi's highly-rated cheeses, selection of essential cured meats, fresh fruit, crackers, and many more of Aldi's must-have products.

Need some ideas? We've got plenty of ways to build the ultimate charcuterie board that stay within this humble budget to to help make you the host with the most. Note that all of the products and prices below are sourced from an Aldi location in southern California and inventory may vary throughout the country, so be sure to double check your local store's online inventory.

If you want to stick to the tried and true, classic charcuterie board ingredients, you can gather all the hits at Aldi for $25 and build a beautiful board. First (and arguable the most important) stop is the cheese. With Aldi's affordable prices, you can feature three different cheeses which will give the board enough variety — ideally, a classic board combines both soft and hard cheese.

Aldi's private-label brand Emporium Selection has three different cheeses that will not only go together lovely, but will satisfy different tastes and preferences: The Garlic & Herb Gourmet Spreadable Cheese, the Smoked Gouda Cheese, and the Aged Reserved White Cheddar Cheese (it's America's favorite cheese, after all).

When it comes to the meat, you can't go wrong with a Salami Trio; you'll get the most bang for your buck here by being able to offer three different types of salami on your board (Black Peppercorn, Smoked Calabrese, and Double Smoked Salami). And now that you have the main events, it's just a matter of filling the board in with two more essential items. Grapes will add some freshness and sweetness, complimenting the salty meat and cheese, Aldi's Rosemary Flatbread Crackers will be the perfect accompaniment for everything else.

If you're looking to serve up something more seasonal, Aldi is full of great fall finds that will work splendidly on a charcuterie board. And thanks to the extremely reasonable prices, you can actually cram a lot of different items onto this board so that it's overflowing with fall flavors.

Starting with your cheeses, three seasonal picks will be the centerpieces: a Cheddar Parmesan Cheese ($3.95) that will go with all of your other flavors, a 1,000 Day Aged Gouda ($3.99) for that sharp bite, and a Crimson Cranberry White Stilton ($4.19) to really bring it home. For the meat, Aldi's Honey & Bourbon Cocktail Salami ($3.29) is the perfect choice to bring in some of those comforting fall notes.

Candied Pecans ($4.39) and Fig Fruit Spread ($3.29) will add some sweetness to the board, and you can brighten things up a bit with a few fresh seasonal Bartlett Pears ($3.29). Grab some of Aldi's Sea Salt Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) that'll work perfectly with any combo, and you've got yourself one great fall-flavored charcuterie board.

Are you cooking up an Italian dinner, or just in the mood for some salty, briny antipasti appetizers? You can create a charcuterie board version of Italian antipasti with several Italian-inspired favorites that you can find at Aldi, and snack like you're in Italy while keeping it all under $25.

For your cheese selection, a fresh log of mozzarella cheese ($3.25) will be the perfect counterpart to the nutty, salty authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano ($6.05) (which is different from Parmesan). And with several types of Italian-imported cured meats available, you can offer up some options like Priano's Prosciutto Italiano ($3.55) and Speck Italiano ($3.55).

Outside of the meat and cheese, Aldi actually has a ready-made medley of antipasti olives ($2.85) which includes black and green pitted olives, provolone cheese cubes, button mushrooms, and roasted red peppers — giving your board lots of variety and bang for your buck. Aldi's Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) is the perfect dip-able, spreadable item to accompany everything, along with some Sea Salt & Olive Oil Italian Breadsticks ($2.19) for crispy, crunchy bites.

If you're feeling a little French, bring some French countryside charm to a rustic charcuterie board using an array of Aldi products that will give your guests a little taste of France. Because who doesn't want that?

You can go for the French trifecta of cheeses for this one: a double creme brie ($4.39), a buttery camembert ($4.39), and a smoked Gruyere ($4.39). This will give your board a mix of soft and hard cheeses, each with its own unique flavor to keep the tastebuds on their toes. Stick to a classic salami to compliment the bolder flavors of the cheese, and if you want to level things up you can always bake the brie (which you can even do in your microwave).

Then include some classic French ingredients for those added touches that'll transport you to France. Aldi's Herb Cornichons ($3.29) and Burman's Sweet Honey Dijon Mustard ($1.75) will taste delicious served alongside your meat and cheese, and then you can freshen things up a bit with red grapes ($1.69 / pound). Now all you need is the perfect vehicle to carry all of these French goodies: Aldi's Original Brioche Style Mini Toasts ($1.89).

One last stop in the Mediterranean. You can combine all of the delicious Mediterranean-inspired items at Aldi to build a board that transforms charcuterie into a delectable mezze spread.

When it comes to the cheese, there's one clear star here: feta. You can represent it two ways in one board by grabbing the Tomato and Basil Feta Cheese Block ($3.95) and the Greek Feta Salad ($2.59) (made with Kalamata and green olives and cubes of feta marinated in herbs and spices). And the Dry Aged Fennel Mediterranean Style Salami ($3.99) is the no-brainer choice for this board's protein.

From there, focus on the delicious dips that make mezze what it is. Go for Aldi's Olive Tapenade Hummus ($2.85) to double down on those salty olives, and brighten up the board with a Cucumber Dill Tzatziki Dip ($3.29) made with Greek yogurt. Throw in some Deli-Sliced Roasted Red Peppers ($3.19) as an accompaniment, and don't forget everyone's favorite part: The pita bread ($2.85)! Pro tip: Throw 'em in the oven for a few minutes and serve them warm; it makes all the difference.

Make the holidays even more festive with a holiday-themed charcuterie board that'll look (and taste) the part. Whether you're looking to serve something beautiful at your holiday party or you want to dive into those festive flavors while you can, Aldi has tons of options to choose from that scream holiday season.

Start with Aldi's Cranberry Cinnamon Flavored Goat Cheese Log ($3.85) (because what says holiday more than that combo?), and balance it out with the Cabot Seriously Sharp Cheddar Cheese for that sharpness everyone wants on a charcuterie board, plus some extra creaminess in the Double Crème Brie Cheese ($4.39). For the cured meat, you can stick with a classic prosciutto ($3.59), and accompany the main events with some warm and cozy flavors like Aldi's Caramelized Red Onion Chutney ($2.99) for sweetness and Honey Roasted Nut Blend ($5.29) for extra crunch.

Pair everything with Aldi's Rosemary Artisan Crackers ($3.49) (bonus points if you have some real rosemary to use as decor). And, last but not least, choose a tasty whole pomegranate ($1.89) to give your board a pop of sweetness as well as a pop of color — leave one half in tact and place it on your board cut-side open; it'll look beautiful. Here's how to pick the best pomegranate for your board.

Okay, so this may not technically qualify as a charcuterie board, but that term tends to be very forgiving these days. For all those veggie lovers out there, you can build a meatless, vegetable-forward board at Aldi that'll give everyone a fresh taste of the garden and still keep things interesting.

Aldi's Roasted Garlic & Tomato Basil Monterey Jack Cheese ($3.49) and Onion & Chive Double Gloucester Cheese ($4.19) are a great duo to anchor this board, and a Spinach Artichoke Dip ($2.99) adds even more flavor and creaminess. Along with Aldi's Garden Vegetable Crackers ($1.79), you can serve up all of your herby, cheesy goodness with some fresh crudités using Gourmet Mixed Baby Carrots ($2.99) (which happen to be adorable) and a pound of radishes ($1.45) for added crisp and color. For that last flavorful munch, throw in the Garlic & Herb Nut Blend ($5.29), which includes seasoned pecans, almonds, and cashews.

Charcuterie can be a morning thing too! When it comes to brunch, pretty much anything goes... so why not turn the meal into a flavorful board of breakfast delights? This one gets a little creative and combines sweet, salty, herby, and smoky for the perfect brunch munching.

Instead of your typical bread or crackers, you can build this board around Aldi's mini bagels ($3.85), which will be the perfect vehicle for soft, herby cheeses like everybody's favorite Boursin Garlic & Fine Herb Cheese ($6.05) and a Chive & Onion Cream Cheese Spread ($1.99). Make it a lox party by adding some of Aldi's Cold Smoked Atlantic Salmon ($4.39) so your guests can create their perfect combo. To round it all out, opt for the jam or preserves of your choice (we like blueberry preserves, $3.09) and incorporate some fresh blackberries ($1.69) to give everyone their morning serving of fruit.

Some like it hot, and those people can find plenty of options at Aldi to set their mouths on fire. Make things (painfully) fun with a spiced-up charcuterie board featuring some of Aldi's hot and spicy products.

Begin the spice-loving journey with Aldi's 3 Chili Gouda Cheese ($3.85) paired with the Tequila & Ghost Pepper Cocktail Salami ($3.29): A killer combo. Next, grab the Stuffed Green Pepperoncini ($3.99) — these will be a great addition because they're a little briny and spicy, but they're made with Herbes de Provence and filled with cream cheese, which will offer a bit of a respite from the heat.

Now for the dips, include the Hot Honey Dip ($2.79) for a bit of sweet heat, and the Piquillo Pepper & Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) for another delicious element that offers a bit more sweetness than spice to balance things out. Finish it all off with Aldi's Sea Salt & Pepper Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) for dipping and dunking.

Pickled and pickle-flavored foods seem to be all the rage lately, so why not lean in? Turn your party into a pickle party by building a fully pickled-out charcuterie board at Aldi for that punchy hit of briny, vinegary goodness.

Two types of cheese will be at the center of the pickle party: the Dill Havarti Cheese ($2.75) (a creamy Danish-style cheese) will keep you on theme while the Extra Sharp New York Cheddar Cheese Cubes ($3.29) will cut all that vinegar with salty sharpness. The Appleton Farms Gourmet Deli Selection ($5.89) is a great choice for your cured meat because it gives you three types of meat in one package (Pepper Salami, Hot Capocollo, and Hot Calabrese).

#9629. Add This Fresh Herb To Your Bowl Of Chili For 10x The Flavor (Thanks, Ina Garten)

A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions. You can make the dish red or green, use proteins like turkey, pork, or chicken instead of the classic beef, and include many aromatics in the mix. Each detail makes a chili rendition unique. Even a fresh herb gives a bowl a whole new character — just look toward Ina Garten's inclusion of basil. Ina Garten often uses basil as a swap for cilantro, so her inclusion of the herb in her chili makes sense.

Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well. Garten uses basil's mildly citrusy sweet and lightly peppery flavor specifically in a chicken-based chili, integrating the herb during both the initial simmering stage and as a final garnish. It's a one-two combo that establishes an herbal character that infuses into every bite, lending more than just a basil-inflected finish.

Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition. Still, seasonings like cumin, chili powder, and a dash of spicy cayenne appear in the mix, cementing the dish as a bowl of chili, only brighter and more herbal in nature.

Ina Garten's tips for cooking chicken perfectly dependably deliver, but don't rule out employing the basil in chili recipes with other proteins, too. The herb also works well in an extra-hearty bean and brisket rendition that's spiced with chiles and even coffee. Cooked down right alongside the kidney beans, basil lends the legumes its distinct herbal character, all without becoming a cornerstone flavor. You can try out such a technique in a classic ground beef chili, too; using the herb early in cooking makes it one of many layered flavors.

If you're after a more basil-forward spin, consider working the herb into a ground turkey chili recipe. You can still go heavy on the spice, using chili powder and jalapeños alongside garlic powder and cumin. Add dried basil early on and raw basil atop the finished chili, and you'll get a delicate bowl, herbal-tasting and fresh, yet still pretty classic.

And for a more inventive approach, take a page from Thai cuisine, specifically Phat ka-phrao (stir-fried basil beef). Made with sturdier Thai basil, this version of the herb stands up better to heat. Saute the meat alongside extra-spicy chiles, lots of garlic, and this type of basil, and you can lay down the foundation for an extra-bold chili, still delicious over rice or with tortilla chips.

#9627. Stop Fixing Vulnerabilities in Production — Fix Them Where They're Born

I am a Principal Engineer with over 19 years of experience designing secure, scalable, and high-performance

I am a Principal Engineer with over 19 years of experience designing secure, scalable, and high-performance

I am a Principal Engineer with over 19 years of experience designing secure, scalable, and high-performance

Most production vulnerabilities are not introduced in production — they are introduced in the Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

Yet historically, most security tooling has operated after code is written, after pull requests are merged, or even worse — after deployment. This reactive approach creates costly rework cycles, slows down release velocity, and increases organizational security risk.

Modern DevSecOps fundamentally changes this model. Security must exist inside the developer workflow, not outside of it.

Over the past decade, the software supply chain threat landscape has evolved dramatically. Organizations today face risk not only from insecure application code, but also from Open-source dependency vulnerabilities, License compliance violations, misconfigured cloud resources, Insecure CI/CD automation pipelines, compromised build artifacts, & Malicious dependency injection attacks.

As organizations accelerate toward microservices, cloud-native architectures, and rapid release cycles, traditional security checkpoints are no longer sufficient. Security must become continuous, automated, and developer-centric. There is always a risk when you try to push a bug fix in production overnight, and you overlook security checks in place, which can expose your production system.

The most critical data an organization must safeguard is its customers’ information—whether PII or CPNI. Failure to protect this data can expose customers to risk and lead to serious legal, financial, and reputational consequences for the organization.

This article describes a pragmatic and scalable approach to secure development using:

SonarQube — Real-time SAST and code quality enforcement inside the IDE

The majority of vulnerabilities are introduced during coding. Developer-focused security ensures issues are detected at the earliest possible stage — when they are cheapest and fastest to fix.

Common vulnerabilities introduced during development include:

·       Improper authorization or missing access validation

When detected early, these issues can be fixed before code review, build, or deployment phases.

Modern tools like SonarQube and Xray help developers understand security risks directly within their development workflow, while AI assistants like GitHub Copilot help apply secure coding fixes quickly and consistently.

In large enterprise environments — particularly telecom and financial systems — early detection directly helps with lower remediation costs, fewer production incidents, faster release cycles, and higher developer productivity.

SonarQube is a real-time code quality and security analysis tool that runs inside your IDE (like VS Code, IntelliJ, Eclipse). It helps developers detect bugs, security vulnerabilities, and code smells as they write code—before it even reaches CI/CD. It can help with:

You can use SonarQube for Java, Python, JavaScript, C#, C++, and many other programming languages.

·       Real-time linting to show real-time code issues the developer can fix.

·       Autofix suggestions while the developer is coding.

·       SonarQube connects to enterprise SonarQube using “Connected Mode.” In this mode, the developer’s IDE pulls the same quality profile, rules, and project settings used by SonarQube.

·       Mandatory security rule set (OWASP Top 10 + CWE)

When developers keep these features enabled, they ensure there are no vulnerable code submissions, that developers adhere to enterprise security guidelines, and that the SAST baseline is unified.

SonarQube shows hazardous code as Security Hotspots, e.g.: Missing or insufficient input validation

·       Potentially unsafe regular expressions

Security hotspots should be triaged and resolved before code review, reducing downstream review cycles and preventing security backlog accumulation.

The screenshot below shows a catch block issue flagged by SonarQube. In this example, the first catch block handles the parent Exception class, and the second handles a subclass — which can never be reached.

- uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@v2

Across telecom and financial platforms, internal security analytics often show:

This reinforces why shift-left security is essential, not optional.

Modern applications rely heavily on open-source software. While this accelerates development, it introduces external risk exposure.

·       Dependency manifest and SBOM generation

·       Real-time notifications about critical vulnerabilities

·       Auto-create JIRA tickets for remediation

·       Apply auto-suggest patch versions

·       Zero trust supply chain methodologies

Artificial Intelligence-assisted development: AI-assisted development allows developers to remediate vulnerabilities faster by generating secure code patterns based on context and security rules.

Example Prompt in VS Code that shows the SQL Injection:

Below screenshot: fixing the vulnerability; green-highlighted is the new code which is added by Copilot

“Instead, replace this outdated MD5 hashing logic with a robust algorithm such as SHA-256 or Argon2.”

“Write Java Spring Boot code for input validation concerning length, type, and sanitized inputs.”

“When SonarQube points out that a rule has been violated, the message should be copied, and the following question asked”

“Rewrite the code in compliance with the SonarQube rule S2068 (Remove hardcoded credentials).”

Copilot can also suggest secure configuration patterns beyond code-level fixes.

·       SonarQube → insecure coding detection in real time

·       Copilot → provides secure remediation instantly

·       Xray → OSS scanning, dependency scanning

·       Automatically route SonarQube and Xray findings back to the responsible developer

·       Leverage developer SDKs to surface security metrics within existing tooling

·       Enforce release governance policies that block deployments failing security thresholds

This helps to ensure that a continuous and closed-loop secure development process is created.

·       Apply Copilot coding patterns safely

·       Do not hardcode credentials or secrets

·       All external inputs must be validated

· Block releases of code for critical SAST/OSS findings

· Train developers to follow secure coding standards (OWASP and CWE)

·       Drive remediation through standardized secure coding patterns and automated policy enforcement.

The future of secure software development will be shaped by deeper integration within developer tools, AI-assisted coding, and automated security governance. Security signals will be embedded directly into IDEs, giving developers real-time, contextual risk awareness as they write code.

There will be an increase in the role of AI in the identification of insecure patterns, remediation, and potential prediction of security issues that will occur, via coding and dependency usage patterns. At the same time, organizations will likely strengthen their models of zero trust for supply chains, which will necessitate verification of software, signed software, and overall validation of compliance.

The organizations that will succeed are those that treat security as a developer experience issue, not only as a security team problem.

Secure development is no longer optional — it is foundational to modern software engineering.

·       JFrog Xray (Supply Chain Security)

·       GitHub Copilot (AI-Driven Secure Remediation)

·       Scale secure development across distributed teams

Security must move from pipeline-only enforcement to IDE-first security.

AI is not replacing security review — it is accelerating secure development.

Open-source supply chain risk is now one of the primary breach vectors. Organizations that embed security directly into developer workflows will achieve both faster delivery velocity and stronger security posture.

How Solution Architects Can Use Generative AI Without Losing Architectural Judgement

#9626. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9624. Upgrade Tuna Salad With A Boxed Ingredient That Improves Texture

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Tuna salad is a pragmatic yet delicious dish, easily crafted using pantry staples. Open up some canned fish packed in oil or water, mix with store-bought mayo, then fold in some aromatics, and you'll have yourself a tasty classic. It's a tried-and-true formula that welcomes many other shelf-stable components, like panko bread crumbs, for example. You only need about 2 tablespoons per can of tuna to round things out nicely.

The delicate breadcrumb style is wonderfully versatile in the kitchen, and its texture enhances tuna salad, too. The foodstuff lends the dish more body, without turning it too dense. The panko absorbs moisture, making the crumbs turn soft while still retaining airiness, in turn creating an extra-tender salad. The panko also thickens the dish, giving your meal more structure. Not to mention, a bite here or there might still remain crunchy, upping the textural intrigue.

It's an advantageous set of qualities unique specifically to panko; you won't want to reach for a different breadcrumb in this application, as they may be too dense. This Japanese foodstuff is made using a unique electric cooking process, producing a delicate crumble without any bread crust. Other breadcrumb varieties are simply too heavy for the task. So grab a package of panko online or in stores to make a tuna salad rendition with a textural twist.

Not sure how to round out a tuna salad with panko? The options are wide-ranging. You could keep to a straightforward mix of tuna, mayo, salt, and pepper — perfect for a tuna sandwich filling — or go with the many potential tuna salad upgrades. Walnuts or kimchi, for example, add body and even more texture to the dish.

Similarly, to complement panko's delicate composition, throw in some vegetables. Green onion, celery, and an herb, say parsley, dill, or cilantro, are tried-and-true tuna salad enhancements. And don't overlook a tangy fermented bite, whether in the form of pickles or pickled onions for a truly amped up tuna salad. You could also imbue brightness using vinegar or even lime juice, which will aromatically soak into the panko.

Alternatively, consider playing to the breadcrumb's East Asian origins, using other Japanese ingredients in the dish. You could add a couple spoonfuls of miso into the dressing for complex savory flavors, as well as sesame seeds and oil for a discernible nutty touch. Or go down the spicy tuna route, incorporating a hot sauce like Sriracha into the build — especially tasty when wrapped in seaweed. Swap the standard mayo for a Japanese-style emulsion, mix in the panko, and you'll have yourself a magical tuna salad foundation.

#9621. Scrambled Eggs Get A Major Protein And Flavor Boost When You Add This Omega-Rich Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When many of us think "hot breakfast," we tend to naturally gravitate toward thoughts of scrambled eggs. Aside from the fact that, when prepared correctly, they are tender, delicate, and fluffy (or custardy, depending on how you like them), eggs are considered the gold standard for protein, so they are quite wholesome as well. On their own, though, they can get a little monotonous, especially if you're making them every day, so it does help to add an ingredient here or there. And if you happen to enjoy omega-3-rich cold-smoked salmon, well, it pairs seamlessly with a classic scramble, boosting both the flavor and the protein content.

Once considered an expensive delicacy, smoked salmon is quite popular now in the U.S., and as a result, it's much easier to find at your local grocery store (even Aldi carries its own version, and it can be found at Walmart, too). Cold-smoked salmon, despite the fact that it tends to be packed in super-thin slices, is buttery and velvety. While it does taste fishy, there are also light, smoky notes that give it a deeply savory flavor, which works beautifully when combined with the mild egg scramble. Additionally, a serving (which will vary in size) might contain anywhere from 12 to 18 grams of protein, which is great if you have daily goals you want to meet or you're just looking to get more of the macronutrient in general.

Truly, the most difficult part about incorporating smoked salmon into your scramble is cooking the eggs to the right consistency without burning or browning them. All you have to do with the salmon is slice the ultra-thin pieces into slivers or small squares. Once your eggs have reached the texture you desire, you'll take the pan off the heat and fold in the salmon. That's literally it; you don't have to actually cook the salmon over direct heat because it's so delicate that the residual warmth of the scrambled eggs will gently bring it up to temperature.

Now, because smoked salmon is so light and thin, you might want your eggs to match that energy, so create a fluffy, soft texture with a bit of cream whisked in. Alternatively, you could take a page out of Bobby Flay's book and fold in a dollop of crème fraîche, or really up the decadence and melt in some cubes of cream cheese (and take care not to overcook anything, because smoked salmon with burnt, rubbery eggs? No thanks). Also, because all of the elements involved are either rich or thick, a sprinkling of something green, like fresh chives or dill, or even a little parsley or tarragon, would brighten things up, both aesthetically and in terms of flavor.

#9620. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9617. Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

Indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

While it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

With ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

Remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.

#9614. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9611. This Chain Serves The Best Old-School Italian Sub, According To Customer Reviews

You might not expect it, but sandwich chains are holding it down when it comes to Italian subs. Of course, there is no denying the appeal of a small, locally owned shop, but there are many reasons why you might opt instead to head into a chain to get your Italian hoagie fix, the most obvious of which is proximity. But there is also the fact that some chains just make darn good food. Food Republic did its research and compiled a list of the best chain Italian subs based on customer reviews, and each entry brings its own unique flavor to the table. But only one, the No. 13 Original Italian from Jersey Mike's, can claim to be the best old-school version of this particular sub.

"They do it right," one Reddit user said, referencing the Original Italian. They continued by stating that if they had a classic Italian deli near them, they'd go there, but since they don't, "it's Jersey Mike's without question." Another user in that same thread agreed, writing, "I love this sub and am always a little amazed [it comes from] a chain" and not, presumably, from a traditional deli. And over on Google, a reviewer shared that the Original Italian reminded them of a sub they'd had during their childhood and expressed their gratitude that "there is a place that can make a real Italian hero like the old days."

It's worth noting that an old-school-style Italian sub owes it all to the Italian immigrants who populated this country throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. There are a few stories about how the hoagie came to be, including one based in Philadelphia (where it's the official sandwich of the city) involving shipyard workers and their distinctive lunches. There is another version that describes how Giovanna Amato sold filling sandwiches to dockworkers in Maine. Whatever its origins, the classic Italian sub came to be characterized by Italian meats and cheeses, a variety of fresh, crisp vegetables, a savory dressing, and an oily, vinegary drizzle.

Jersey Mike's Original Italian proves a chain can still honor those old-school roots. It checks every box, from five different Italian meats to provolone cheese to the default setting, Mike's Way, which includes onions, lettuce sliced super-thin, and tomatoes, as well as red wine vinegar and an olive oil blend, plus two impactful seasonings: salt and oregano.

But of course, Jersey Mike's serves 21st-century customers who like having options, so the sandwich, in addition to scratching an old-school itch, can also serve as a jumping-off point for some. You might, for example, upgrade your Original Italian sub by choosing the rosemary parmesan bread instead of plain white. There are a number of additional toppings available as well, such as jalapeño peppers, dill pickles, and hot chopped pepper relish.

#9608. Skip Gruyère: This Norwegian Cheese Boasts Nutty Flavor & Fewer Calories

Cheese is one of life's greatest pleasures, but no two varieties are quite the same. Knowing your way around your mozzarella and parmesan is a useful skill that won't just impress your dinner guests but will also transform the way you use cheese in the kitchen. Take Gruyère, for example. If, say, a French onion soup recipe calls for it, and you've had no luck finding it at the store, any cheese connoisseur will tell you that Norwegian Jarlsberg makes an excellent substitute. The two share a similar nutty flavor and melt beautifully, with Jarlsberg also serving a lower-calorie option.

Jarlsberg is instantly recognizable thanks to its large, round holes, and while traditional Swiss Gruyère might lack these holes, it matches Jarlsberg's intensely nutty flavor — although how the two cheeses develop their respective flavors is very different. Jarlsberg gets it from a proprietary bacterial culture called Propionibacterium shermanii, a sub-sect of Propionibacterium freudenreichii. During fermentation, this culture consumes lactic acid to produce propionic acid and carbon dioxide. The acid contributes to the cheese's nutty profile, while the carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the cheese, creating those large holes. Gruyère takes a different approach, developing its signature flavor through a combination of factors, including the unique composition of the high-altitude Alpine milk, its bacterial cultures, and a longer aging process.

Despite sharing a similar taste, their nutritional profiles tell a different story. Jarlsberg contains around 100 calories per ounce, compared with up to 120 calories for Gruyère. That's a modest saving of 20 calories per ounce, which can quickly add up if you're using a generous amount in a grilled cheese or fondue. So if you're looking for a slightly lighter alternative to Gruyère without sacrificing flavor, Jarlsberg makes for a wonderful swap.

As is the case with Gruyère, one of Jarlsberg's biggest selling points is its versatility. You can always enjoy it as is, pairing it with grapes, crackers, and cold cuts as part of an elegantly presented charcuterie board, or keep things simple and serve it alongside a glass of wine; Jarlsberg goes particularly well with chardonnay and sweet rieslings, as well as low-tannin reds like pinot noir. While there are plenty of ways to enjoy the cheese without cooking it, we think the best way to get the most out of Jarlsberg is to take advantage of its meltability.

Jarlsberg's flavor is comparatively milder than that of sharper Gruyère, making it an excellent substitute if you're after a nutty, creamy cheese that won't overpower everything else, which makes it a great contender for a grilled cheese. If you still want some of Gruyère's intensity, simply combine the two. Their complementary flavor profiles mean neither cheese should overpower the other, giving you a nutty filling with plenty of depth. In a nod to Jarlsberg's Norwegian roots, add in some fresh dill, pickles, and a generous helping of cold-smoked salmon for a Scandi-inspired twist.

Another great way to put Jarlsberg to work is as a pizza topping. Its mild, buttery flavor and excellent meltability make it an obvious fit. Rather than tomato sauce, pair it with mushrooms, caramelized onions, and fresh thyme to let the cheese shine. If white pizza isn't your thing, swap the dough for Danish rye bread to create your own smørbrød, a charming Scandinavian open-faced sandwich. Simply take the buttered bread and add your toppings of choice, layer the Jarlsberg on top, then blast it in the broiler until creamy and gooey.

#9607. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9601. Give Tuna Salad A Flavorful Protein Boost With An Ingredient You Have Stocked In The Fridge

Tuna salad typically already comes with plenty of protein and flavor, but boosting these virtues can give you something even more delicious and nutritionally dense. This is especially true if you use boiled eggs, an easy-to-prepare ingredient that's highly compatible with whatever recipe you prefer.

Exact needs vary based on body type and medical history, but most adults need a minimum of about 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight daily. Beginning a recipe with canned tuna, which hovers around 22 grams of protein per 3-ounce serving, is a good start, but it can be better. A single boiled egg contains roughly 6 grams of protein and is rich in umami, no matter what texture you cook it to. The whites add a lovely, soft chew to counteract the density of fish meat, while the yolks themselves sort of disappear into the mayonnaise to boost its richness.

If you use the best mayo for tuna salad — Kewpie, which is packed with MSG — you'll get an extra umami bomb. Between the fish, egg, and MSG, you have all the makings of a hearty, satisfying meal, whether you eat it straight or heat it up in a melt. The end result is something that tastes more decadent than it does nutritious, full of velvety textures and rich flavors that make it seem like you spent quite a bit of time perfecting your recipe. Combine it all with minced veggies and pickles, and you get something comprehensively nourishing that's ready in a flash.

Eggs can be so much more than simply hard-boiled, so you've got plenty of options when it comes to the exact tastes and textures you want your tuna salad to have. Some bulk out a bowl, some focus on the sauce, and still others can add delightful new textures, but all are quite easy.

If you want something with an unobtrusive texture but a great amount of flavor, then boil your eggs for a jammy yolk. The runnier center diffuses through the mayonnaise, infusing it with flavor before it coats every piece of fish. If you're looking for something different, you can pan-fry hard-boiled eggs to crisp up the exteriors and add a touch of roasted flavor to a comparatively fresh and cool dish. If you use a flavored oil, like chili oil or one infused with herbs, this is an easy way to add new seasonings to the overall dish.

Eggs can either introduce a dichotomy of textures or disappear into the meal, depending on your preference. Leaving your eggs whole or cut in half lets you spoon them into individual bites, preventing your meal from being too one-note. On the other hand, finely dicing them into crumbles is the best way to get their flavor into every nook, cranny, and ingredient. Using an egg slicer can give you the best of both worlds, creating thin slivers of white while the yolk dissolves into the mayonnaise.
